The [Orbital Sciences X-34][ref_x34] was cancelled on the same day, in the same decision and for the same
stated reason as the vehicle in the previous article, and almost nothing else about the two is alike. The
[X-33][related_post_a330_lockheed_martin_x33] was enormous, used liquid hydrogen, carried an untried engine
architecture, and failed a structural test in a way that made a photograph.
**The X-34 was small, burned kerosene, used an engine designed to be cheap rather than good, was finished, was towed and carried through the air by [an airliner turned launch aircraft][ref_stargazer], and was cancelled without anything breaking at all.**
This is the thirty-fifth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_xplanes_framing], following the
[X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the
[X-3][related_post_a300_douglas_x3], the [X-4][related_post_a301_northrop_x4], the
[X-5][related_post_a302_bell_x5], the [X-6][related_post_a303_convair_x6], the

[X-9][related_post_a306_bell_x9], the [X-10][related_post_a307_north_american_x10], the
[X-11][related_post_a308_convair_x11], the [X-12][related_post_a309_convair_x12], the
[X-13][related_post_a310_ryan_x13], the [X-14][related_post_a311_bell_x14], the

[X-31][related_post_a328_rockwell_mbb_x31], the [X-32][related_post_a329_boeing_x32], and the
[X-33][related_post_a330_lockheed_martin_x33].

**The difference that matters is not size or propellant. It is that the two programmes had different kinds of unknown.**
The X-33's binding unknown was mass. Mass obeys a conservation law, a demonstrator can be weighed, and what
came back was a number that did not close. **The X-34's binding unknown was cost, and cost obeys nothing.**

* Contents
{:toc}

## The Research Question

**The keystone is whether cost can be attacked as an engineering quantity, and what it costs to try.**

That is an unusual keystone for this series and the difficulty is worth stating at once. Every previous
article has dimensioned an aircraft against a physical unknown. A drag rise, a heating rate, a divergence
speed, a mass fraction. **Those quantities have units, conservation laws and instruments.** Cost has none of
the three. It has no equation of state, it cannot be measured on the article, and every number attached to
it is a forecast rather than a reading.

### Why That Is Not a Reason to Refuse the Subject

**The cost argument left physical fingerprints, and those can be computed.** A programme that attacks cost
does it by simplifying, and every simplification has a performance price with units. The X-34 chose an
engine cooled by being destroyed, a propellant with a third of the specific energy advantage and three times
the density, an aeroplane to carry it to altitude instead of a launch pad, and a level of system testing
that a later review found insufficient.
**Four of those five choices can be priced in kilograms, seconds and newtons.** The fifth could not be
priced at all until somebody tried to fly the vehicle.

### The Question Behind the Question

**A cheap demonstrator demonstrates that demonstrators can be cheap.** Whether it demonstrates that an
operational vehicle can be cheap is a separate claim and a much weaker one, and the distinction runs through
this whole article.

**The programme's own answer arrived as an arithmetic correction rather than as a test result.** A
restructure plan put the total requirement at about 348 million dollars against roughly 86 million budgeted
in 1996, and the reason given was that reaching an acceptable level of risk needed more system testing, more
government technical insight and more integrated assessment.
**Those are the things a low-cost programme removes.**

## Programme Origin

### What the Agency Wanted and What It Bought

**The X-34 belongs to the same family as the X-33 and answers a different half of the same question.** Both
were technology demonstrators under a [reusable launch vehicle][ref_rlv] programme whose stated ambition was
an order-of-magnitude reduction in the cost of reaching orbit. The X-33 pursued that by attacking the mass
fraction, which is the physics of the problem.
**The X-34 pursued it by attacking the price of the hardware, which is not.**

The contract went to [Orbital Sciences][ref_orbital] in 1996 at a figure near 86 million dollars, which set
it against the X-33 at more than a billion. **A ratio of that size is the argument in a single number**, and
testing whether the ratio survives contact with the vehicles is the work of the Where the Framing Breaks
Down section.

### The Company and the Method

**Orbital Sciences had already done the thing the X-34 needed.** The company operated
[an air-launched satellite booster][ref_pegasus] carried by a modified airliner, so the carrier aircraft,
the release mechanism, the separation problem and the operating culture existed before the X-34 did.
**A programme that reuses an existing carrier does not pay for one**, and that is a real cost argument
rather than a rhetorical one.

### The Engine Nobody Else Would Have Built

**The [Fastrac engine][ref_fastrac], also designated MC-1, was designed by [a government laboratory][ref_msfc] to be cheap.**
It used a [gas generator cycle][ref_gasgen], commercial parts where they would serve, a simplified
turbopump, and a combustion chamber and nozzle cooled not by circulating its own fuel but by being consumed.
**An engine reported at around 1.2 million dollars in its development phase, against a production target near 350,000, is a different kind of object from the one in the previous article**,
and the Sizing section takes it apart.

## Sizing From First Principles

### Three Published Numbers That Do Not Close

**Begin with the engine's own data sheet, because it contains a discrepancy that turns out to be informative.**
The published figures are a vacuum thrust of 60,000 pounds force, a vacuum specific impulse of 314 seconds,
and a total propellant mass flow of 91.90 kilograms per second.

**Those three quantities are related by [the definition of specific impulse][ref_isp].** Writing $F$ for
thrust, $\dot{m}$ for mass flow and $g_0$ for standard gravity,

$$I_{sp} = \frac{F}{\dot{m} \, g_0}$$

which is the form [Sutton sets out for propulsion analysis][book_rocket_propulsion_elements].

Converting the thrust to 266,893 newtons, which is 266.9 kilonewtons, and substituting,

$$I_{sp} = \frac{266{,}893}{91.90 \times 9.80665} = 296.14 \ \text{s}$$

**against a published 314, which is 5.69 percent adrift.** A disagreement of that size in a published pair
is either an error or a distinction, and here it is a distinction.

### The Gap Is the Cycle

**A gas generator engine does not send all its propellant through the nozzle.** A small stream is burned
fuel-rich in a separate chamber to drive the turbopump, and the exhaust from that turbine is dumped
overboard rather than expanded through the main nozzle, where it would contribute thrust.
**So the specific impulse belongs to the chamber flow and the mass flow is what the vehicle's tanks actually lose.**

Writing $\dot{m}_c$ for the chamber flow and $\dot{m}_{gg}$ for the gas generator flow, the chamber flow
follows from the two published performance figures,

$$\dot{m}_c = \frac{F}{I_{sp} \, g_0} = \frac{266{,}893}{314 \times 9.80665} = 86.674 \ \text{kg/s}$$

and the generator flow is the remainder,

$$\dot{m}_{gg} = 91.90 - 86.674 = 5.226 \ \text{kg/s}$$

**which is 5.69 percent of the total.** A gas generator typically spends between three and seven percent of
the propellant it pumps, a range set out in
[Huzel and Huang's design text on liquid propellant rocket engines][book_design_of_liquid_propellant_rocket_eng],
so **an unpublished cycle parameter has been recovered from three published ones**, and it lands inside the
range the architecture actually uses.

**The same arithmetic gives what the cycle costs the vehicle.** The effective specific impulse, the one the
rocket equation sees, is 296.14 seconds against a chamber value of 314, so

$$\Delta I_{sp} = 314 - 296.14 = 17.86 \ \text{s}$$

**The two percentages are identical and that is not a coincidence.** The fractional impulse the cycle costs
equals the fractional flow the cycle takes, exactly, because both are one minus the same ratio. The identity
was tested over twenty thousand randomised combinations of thrust, flow and impulse without a failure.

### A Fourth Number That Closes on the Other Three

**The vehicle's propellant load and the engine's flow rate give a burn time**, and it can be checked against
the longest engine test the programme published.

$$t_b = \frac{m_p}{\dot{m}} = \frac{13{,}600}{91.90} = 148.0 \ \text{s}$$

**against a longest published hot fire of 155 seconds, a margin of 1.047.** The masses, the flow rate and
the test duration were published separately and by different parts of the programme, and they describe one
vehicle burning one propellant load with about five percent to spare.
**Had the tested duration come out below the mission burn, one of the four numbers would have been wrong.**

### What the Vehicle Could Actually Reach

**The draft of this article computed the engine and never asked what the vehicle does with it**, and the
answer is a check on the published masses. The effective exhaust velocity is the effective impulse times
standard gravity,

$$v_e = I_{sp,\text{eff}} \, g_0 = 296.14 \times 9.80665 = 2{,}904.2 \ \text{m/s}$$

**which is 2,904.2 metres per second.** The mass ratio is the release mass over the burnout mass,

$$\frac{m_0}{m_f} = \frac{21{,}800}{8{,}200} = 2.6585$$

so the ideal velocity increment is

$$\Delta v = v_e \ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right) = 2{,}839.6 \ \text{m/s}$$

**The ideal increment is 2,839.6 metres per second, and adding the 236.1 the carrier aircraft already supplied gives 3,075.7**,
against a Mach 8 objective which at the burnout altitude is about 2,400 metres per second.

$$3{,}075.7 - 2{,}400 = 675.7 \ \text{m/s}$$

**leaving 675.7 metres per second, or 22.0 percent of the ideal total, for gravity, drag and steering.** A
vehicle whose ideal increment exceeded its objective by only a few percent would be claiming no losses at
all, and one that exceeded it by half would suggest an objective set well below what the vehicle could do.
**Twenty-two percent is what a suborbital ascent actually spends**, which is a check on the published masses
rather than on the trajectory.

**The thrust to weight at release follows from the same figures,**

$$\frac{F}{m_0 g_0} = \frac{266{,}893}{21{,}800 \times 9.80665} = 1.248$$

**and a vehicle released in level flight needs no more than one**, because the wing is already carrying it.
Being above one is what lets an air-launched vehicle pitch up immediately rather than sinking while it
accelerates.

The propellant mass fraction follows from the same masses,

$$\zeta = \frac{13{,}600}{21{,}800} = 0.6239$$

**or 62.4 percent, against 73.7 for the X-33 and the 89.0 percent an orbital vehicle needs.** The X-34 is
further from an orbital mass fraction than the X-33 was, and neither was required to be close, because
neither was going anywhere near orbit.
**That is worth saying plainly, because the temptation with a demonstrator is to read its numbers as predictions of the vehicle it stood for.**

### The Chamber That Is Consumed

**The Fastrac's combustion chamber and nozzle were cooled [ablatively][ref_ablative].** There is no
[regenerative jacket][ref_regen] circulating fuel through passages in the wall. Instead a silica-phenolic
liner inside a composite overwrap absorbs heat by decomposing, and the gas that leaves the decomposing
surface keeps the hot flow off the wall. **The wall survives by being destroyed at a controlled rate.**

**That is a genuine cost argument**, and the manufacturing burden it avoids is set out in
[the same design text][book_design_of_liquid_propellant_rocket_eng]. A regeneratively cooled chamber is a
precision assembly of hundreds of brazed passages, and it is one of the most expensive parts of a rocket
engine to make. An ablative liner is a moulding.

**It has a consequence that the words reusable launch vehicle do not prepare anyone for.** Taking the
chamber flow and the characteristic velocity, the throat area follows from

$$A_t = \frac{\dot{m}_c \, c^{\ast}}{p_c}$$

and with a chamber pressure of 633 pounds per square inch, or 4.364 megapascals, and an assumed
[characteristic velocity][ref_cstar] of 1,780 metres per second for liquid oxygen and
[RP-1 kerosene][ref_rp1],

$$A_t = \frac{86.674 \times 1{,}780}{4.364 \times 10^6} = 0.03535 \ \text{m}^2$$

a throat 0.212 metres across, and a vacuum thrust coefficient of

$$C_F = \frac{F}{p_c A_t} = 1.7299$$

**Those two quantities divide the engine's performance between its two halves**, since the characteristic
velocity describes everything upstream of the throat and the thrust coefficient everything downstream,

$$I_{sp} = \frac{C_F \, c^{\ast}}{g_0}$$

**That relation is shown for its structure and not as a check.** The throat area above was derived from the
same thrust and impulse, so multiplying the two factors returns them by construction, and presenting the
agreement as confirmation would be circular.

The area ratio then fixes the exit,

$$A_e = \varepsilon A_t = 15 \times 0.03535 = 0.5302 \ \text{m}^2$$

**an exit 0.822 metres across**, which is a check on the assumed ratio, because a nozzle wider than the
vehicle would say the assumption was wrong.

#### How Fast the Wall Is Destroyed, Which Is Not an Assumption

**A recession rate is the output of an energy balance rather than an input to one**, and the balance is
worth running because it fails in an instructive way.

**Start with the heat the wall has to survive.** The standard estimate for a rocket throat is the Bartz
correlation, which gives the gas-side heat transfer coefficient as

$$h_g = \frac{0.026}{D_t^{0.2}}\left(\frac{\mu^{0.2} c_p}{\mathrm{Pr}^{0.6}}\right)\left(\frac{p_c}{c^{\ast}}\right)^{0.8}\left(\frac{D_t}{R_c}\right)^{0.1}$$

With a chamber at about 3,500 kelvin and gas properties typical of liquid oxygen burning with kerosene, that
gives 8,330 watts per square metre per kelvin. The heat arriving is the coefficient times the difference
between the recovery temperature and the ablating surface,

$$q = h_g \left(T_{aw} - T_w\right) = 8{,}330 \times \left(3{,}150 - 1{,}900\right) = 10.41 \ \text{MW/m}^2$$

**Ten megawatts per square metre is the order of magnitude a rocket throat delivers.** The correlation is
good to perhaps a factor of two and that is stated because what follows depends on it.

**Now the balance.** A surface protecting itself by being destroyed removes heat at a rate set by how much
energy each kilogram carries away, so writing $H_{\text{eff}}$ for that effective heat of ablation and
$\rho_a$ for the material density,

$$\dot{s} = \frac{q}{\rho_a H_{\text{eff}}}$$

**Run it forwards with the energy the material can actually absorb.** Heating silica phenolic from room
temperature to 1,900 kelvin takes about 1.76 megajoules per kilogram and vaporising the silica about 12, so

$$H_{\text{absorb}} = 13.76 \ \text{MJ/kg} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \dot{s} = 0.445 \ \text{mm/s}$$

**which over the 148 second burn is 65.9 millimetres, and that is absurd.** A throat losing that much would
not survive, and ablative chambers of this class do not behave that way.

**So invert it.** Chambers of this kind recede at something nearer a tenth of a millimetre per second, and
putting that in gives

$$H_{\text{eff}} = \frac{q}{\rho_a \dot{s}} = \frac{10.41 \times 10^6}{1{,}700 \times 10^{-4}} = 61.3 \ \text{MJ/kg}$$

**against 13.76 that the material can absorb, a ratio of 4.5.**

**The ablator is not mostly absorbing the heat. It is blocking it.** Pyrolysis gas leaving the decomposing
surface blows into the boundary layer and thickens it, cutting the heat that arrives in the first place.
**Absorption is the small term and transpiration is the large one**, by roughly a factor of four, and that
is why an ablative wall works at all rather than merely melting.

**The forward calculation being wrong by that factor is the result**, and it is why a recession rate is
measured rather than predicted.

**The Bartz correlation and the ablation balance are standard results and are not this article's.** What is
this article's is the inversion, which is arithmetic on the balance rather than a new relation, and the
observation that the factor between the two answers is the transpiration term.

**Both halves rest on literatures older than the programme.** The convective heat transfer to a rocket
nozzle was correlated in the late 1950s and the transpiration and mass-injection work that explains the
blocking term runs alongside it, so the physics the X-34's chamber depended on was forty years settled when
the engine was designed.

#### What That Costs the Chamber

At a tenth of a millimetre per second the liner loses

$$\Delta s = \dot{s} \, t_b = 10^{-4} \times 148.0 = 14.8 \ \text{mm}$$

over a full burn, so a chamber built to fly one mission is centimetres thick in its consumable layer and
that layer is gone at the end of it.

| Recession rate | Liner consumed over the burn |
|---|---|
| 0.05 mm per second | 7.4 mm |
| 0.10 mm per second | 14.8 mm |
| 0.15 mm per second | 22.2 mm |
| 0.20 mm per second | 29.6 mm |

**The engine's combustion chamber was a consumable on a vehicle whose entire purpose was reuse**, and the
programme said so plainly, replacing the chamber and the ignition cartridge after each flight while reusing
the rest.
**At the planned rate of twenty-five flights a year, that is twenty-five combustion chambers a year.**

**Whether that is cheap depends entirely on what a chamber costs, which is the article's keystone arriving as a component.**
A moulding at a few tens of thousands of dollars makes it obviously right. A moulding at a few hundred
thousand makes it obviously wrong. **The public record does not contain the number**, and the Epistemic
State says so rather than guessing.

### What Air Launch Actually Donates

**The X-34 was [carried to altitude under a modified airliner and released][ref_airlaunch], and the usual argument for that is altitude and speed.**
The usual argument is the weakest of the several available.

Taking a release at 38,000 feet, which is 11,582 metres, at Mach 0.8, which is typical of the carrier's
launch profile, the specific energy the aircraft has already supplied is potential plus kinetic,

$$e = g_0 h + \frac{v^2}{2}$$

$$e = 9.80665 \times 11{,}582 + \frac{236.1^2}{2} = 141{,}446 \ \text{J/kg}$$

**The total is 141.4 kilojoules per kilogram.** Expressed as the velocity increment that energy would buy,

$$\Delta v_{\text{equiv}} = \sqrt{2e} = 531.9 \ \text{m/s}$$

**which is 5.7 percent of a 9,300 metre per second orbital budget.** An argument for air launch that rests
on the altitude and the speed is arguing from the smallest of its own benefits.

**The larger measurable benefit is that the nozzle never sees sea level.** Thrust falls below its vacuum
value by the ambient pressure acting over the exit area,

$$F = F_{vac} - p_a A_e$$

so at an assumed area ratio of 15, giving an exit area of 0.5302 square metres, the loss at sea level is
53.73 kilonewtons and at the release altitude only 10.95.
**Launching from altitude recovers 42.78 kilonewtons, which is 16.0 percent of vacuum thrust**, and that is
nearly three times what the altitude and speed donate.

**And the largest benefit is the one this article cannot compute.** An air-launched vehicle needs no launch
pad, no flame trench, no fixed azimuth and no launch window dictated by weather over a single site.
**For a programme whose keystone is cost, the ground infrastructure it never has to build is the argument**,
and it has no equation.

### The Same Trade the Previous Article Answered With Hydrogen

**Two consecutive vehicles in this series answered one question in opposite directions, and the question is which propellant to carry.**

Writing $r$ for the mixture ratio, the bulk density of a propellant combination is

$$\rho_{\text{bulk}} = \left[\frac{1}{1+r}\frac{1}{\rho_f} + \frac{r}{1+r}\frac{1}{\rho_o}\right]^{-1}$$

**For kerosene and oxygen at a mixture ratio of 2.56 that is 1,023.5 kilograms per cubic metre, against 343.3 for hydrogen and oxygen at 5.5, a ratio of 2.982.**

**The fuel share of the propellant mass is fixed by the mixture ratio alone,**

$$\frac{m_f}{m_p} = \frac{1}{1+r} = \frac{1}{3.56} = 0.281$$

**or 28.1 percent, so the X-34 carried 3,820 kilograms of kerosene against 9,780 of oxygen.**

**The previous article's central sentence inverts exactly.** Hydrogen is one seventh of the propellant mass
and 74.5 percent of its volume, so the fuel tank is the vehicle.
**Kerosene is about a quarter of the mass and 35.5 percent of the volume**, so the fuel tank is a tank.

The consequence is easiest to see in the load the X-34 actually carried.

$$\frac{13{,}600}{1{,}023.5} = 13.29 \ \text{m}^3 \qquad \text{against} \qquad \frac{13{,}600}{343.3} = 39.62 \ \text{m}^3$$

**An extra 26.33 cubic metres, on a vehicle 17.68 metres long, is not a packaging problem. It is a different aeroplane.**

### Where the Previous Article's Scale Invariance Stops Holding

**The X-33 article proved that the membrane tank fraction contains no length.** A thin vessel of volume $V$
at pressure $p$ has mass $k \rho_w p V / \sigma$ and holds $\rho_p V$ of propellant, so

$$\frac{m_{\text{tank}}}{m_{\text{prop}}} = \frac{k \, \rho_w \, p}{\sigma \, \rho_p}$$

**and the size cancels.** That cancellation is why a subscale tank was a valid test of a full-scale tank
technology, and it is the strongest thing the previous article had to say about demonstrators.

**It cancels only while stress sets the thickness.** The membrane thickness a pressure demands is

$$t = \frac{pR}{\sigma}$$

which falls with the radius, while the thinnest laminate anybody can lay up does not fall at all. Taking the
same construction and pressure as the previous article so the comparison is controlled, and sizing the walls
by the ordinary structural methods
[Bruhn sets out for flight vehicle structures][book_analysis_and_design_of_flight_vehicle_st],

| Tank | Radius | Membrane thickness needed | Per facesheet | Minimum gauge as a multiple |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X-33 hydrogen tank | 2.15 m | 1.384 mm | 0.692 mm | 1.45 |
| X-34 tank, assumed | 0.75 m | 0.483 mm | 0.241 mm | 4.14 |

**The smaller the tank, the more of its wall is material no load asked for.** Once minimum gauge binds, the
wall thickness stops depending on the pressure at all, and the tank fraction follows in three lines. For a
cylinder of radius $R$ whose wall is two facesheets each at the minimum gauge, the wall mass and the
propellant mass per unit length are

$$m'_{\text{wall}} = \rho_w \left(2 \pi R\right) \left(2 t_{\text{gauge}}\right) \qquad m'_{\text{prop}} = \rho_p \pi R^2$$

so the length and the constant both cancel, leaving

$$\frac{m_{\text{tank}}}{m_{\text{prop}}} = \frac{4 \rho_w t_{\text{gauge}}}{\rho_p R}$$

**which goes as one over the radius instead of being independent of it.** The scaling was tested as a
property over twenty thousand random radii and densities.

| Tank radius | Hydrogen and oxygen | Kerosene and oxygen |
|---|---|---|
| 0.50 m | 3.66% | 1.23% |
| 0.75 m | 2.44% | 0.82% |
| 1.00 m | 1.83% | 0.61% |
| 1.50 m | 1.22% | 0.41% |
| 2.15 m | 0.85% | 0.29% |
| 3.00 m | 0.61% | 0.20% |

**Two things follow and they point in opposite directions.**

**The scale penalty is real, so a small demonstrator's tank is proportionally worse than a large vehicle's and cannot stand in for it.**
The X-33's tank could. The X-34's could not.
**That is the previous article's best argument about demonstrators failing at a smaller size**, and it fails
because of manufacture rather than because of mechanics.

**And the propellant more than pays for it.** At the X-34's assumed tank radius a gauge-limited hydrogen and
oxygen tank is 2.44 percent of the propellant it holds and a kerosene and oxygen tank is 0.82,
**a factor of 2.98 which is exactly the ratio of the two bulk densities.** The small vehicle is penalised by
its size and rescued by what it chose to burn.

## The Vehicle

**The X-34 was a small winged rocket aeroplane, 17.68 metres long with an 8.54 metre span, carried aloft under an airliner and released to fly a suborbital profile to about Mach 8.**
It had a composite airframe with composite propellant tanks, silica tiles and flexible blankets for thermal
protection, and it was to land itself on a runway without a pilot.

The published masses are 21,800 kilograms at release, of which 13,600 kilograms were propellant and 8,200
kilograms the vehicle. **Those three figures close exactly**, which is worth noting only because the
previous article's did not.

### What Was Deliberately Left Out

**The list of things the X-34 did not have is the list a later review objected to**, and reading it forwards
rather than backwards is the honest way to treat it. The vehicle had single-string avionics, meaning no
redundant channel for a failure to fall back on. Its system-level testing was thin. Its automatic landing
had not been validated in flight.

**Every one of those is a defensible choice for a cheap demonstrator and an indefensible one for a vehicle about to be released over inhabited ground.**
The programme did not change its mind about engineering. It changed its mind about which of those two things
it was building.

### Thermal Protection

**The X-34 used silica tiles and flexible insulation blankets** rather than the metallic system the X-33
chose, and the requirement that shaped it was unusual. The vehicle had to survive subsonic flight through
weather, because an air-launched vehicle spends its climb attached to an aeroplane flying through whatever
is between the runway and 38,000 feet. **A launch pad does not fly through rain.**

### Autonomy and Landing

**An unpiloted vehicle that lands on a runway has to be right the first time**, and the X-34 was to
demonstrate automatic landing including in a twenty-knot crosswind, with navigation from a combination of
satellite and inertial systems.

**This is where the cost argument and the risk argument meet most directly.** Automatic landing is cheap to
specify and expensive to prove, because proving it means flying it, and flying it is what the programme had
not yet done when it was asked what its residual risk was.

the Reynolds number gap is correspondingly smaller.

## The Flight Test Record

**There is no powered flight test record. The X-34 never fired its engine in the air.**

### What Actually Happened

The first unpowered airframe was rolled out in 1999 at [the agency's flight research centre][ref_dryden]. It
was towed on the ground behind a vehicle to check its landing gear and low-speed handling, and it was
carried aloft beneath the carrier aircraft on captive flights beginning in June 1999, with further captive
flights that September. **A second airframe was mated to the carrier in 2000.** The engine was tested
extensively on the ground, including a firing of 155 seconds.

**No free flight was ever made, powered or unpowered.** The vehicle was never released from the carrier
aircraft.

### The Review That Ended It

**A joint review in 2000 found that the project needed its approach, scope, budget and schedule redefined**,
and named the risks. They were inadequate system testing, single-string avionics and an unvalidated
automatic landing. Reaching an acceptable level of risk would require more government technical insight,
more hardware testing and integrated systems assessment.

**The restructure plan that followed put the total requirement near 348 million dollars against roughly 86 million budgeted in 1996**,
and the programme was cancelled on 31 March 2001 alongside the X-33, with the agency stating that the
benefits did not justify continued investment and that the funds were needed for
[the initiative that replaced both][ref_sli]. The oversight body
[examined the two cancelled programmes together][ref_gao_x33x34] later that year.

$$\frac{348 - 86}{86} = 3.05$$

**A growth of 305 percent, and the arithmetic is not the interesting part.** What the number measures is.

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**This section normally compares prediction with flight measurement. The X-34 produced no flight measurement at all, so what can be compared is prediction against the only two things the programme did produce, which are ground test results and a revised cost estimate.**

### Where the Ground Tests Agreed With Prediction

**The engine worked.** It was fired repeatedly, including for 155 seconds, which exceeds the 148 second burn
a full propellant load implies. The published thrust, impulse and flow figures are mutually consistent once
the gas generator flow is accounted for, and the recovered generator fraction of 5.69 percent lands inside
the range the cycle architecture uses.
**Nothing in the engine's published numbers indicates a machine that was not doing what it was designed to do.**

**The airframe was built, twice.** It was towed, it was carried, it held together, and the two airframes
outlived the programme by nearly two decades.

### Where Prediction and Outcome Diverged, and It Was Not a Physical Quantity

**The prediction that failed was the cost estimate, and it failed by a factor of four.** No structure broke,
no engine failed, no aerodynamic surprise appeared.
**The quantity that moved was the one with no conservation law.**

**That is a different kind of divergence from any this series has met.** A drag rise that comes in higher
than predicted is a fact about air. A cost estimate that comes in higher than predicted is a fact about what
was left out of the estimate, and the review that produced the new figure said exactly what had been left
out.

### The Comparison the Programme Never Got to Make

**The X-34 was to demonstrate rapid turnaround, and turnaround is the one quantity that would have tested the whole cost argument.**
A vehicle that flies twenty-five times a year with a small crew is a different economic object from one that
flies twice. **The programme never flew once**, so the number that mattered most was never measured, and the
article's Epistemic State says so.

## What the Data Changed

### The Verdict on the Cost Argument, Tested Both Ways

**Take the two programmes cancelled in the same decision and divide what each spent by the mass of vehicle it produced.**
Mass is a poor denominator for cost, and it is used here because it is the one comparable quantity both
programmes published. Cost estimating for space systems has its own methods, set out in
[Wertz and Larson's standard treatment of space mission design][book_space_mission_analysis_and_design], and
none of them is a division by mass.
**The article says that rather than pretending the ratio means more than it does.**

The X-34's release mass of 21,800 kilograms is 48,061 pounds, against 285,000 for the X-33.

$$\frac{112 \times 10^6}{48{,}061} = 2{,}330 \ \text{dollars per pound}$$

$$\frac{1{,}280 \times 10^6}{285{,}000} = 4{,}491 \ \text{dollars per pound}$$

**The X-34 comes to 2,330 dollars per pound against the X-33's 4,491, so on money actually spent the low-cost vehicle was 1.93 times cheaper per pound of vehicle**,
and both programmes ended without a powered flight, so the comparison is between two equivalently incomplete
efforts.

**Now do it with the money it would have taken to fly the thing safely.**

$$\frac{348 \times 10^6}{48{,}061} = 7{,}241 \ \text{dollars per pound}$$

**which is 7,241 dollars per pound, or 1.61 times the X-33's actual spend per pound.** The vehicle built to
be cheap would have cost more per pound to finish than the vehicle everyone remembers as the expensive one.

**Both figures are published and they answer different questions.** The first says the programme was
genuinely economical at building hardware.
**The second says that building hardware was not the expensive part.**

### What the Programme Settled

**It settled that a small air-launched reusable demonstrator can be built for a fraction of the cost of a large one**,
which was never seriously in doubt and which the airframes themselves prove.

**It settled that an ablatively cooled engine of that class can be built and run**, and the Fastrac was
fired far more than the X-34 ever flew.

**It did not settle anything about the cost of an operational reusable launch vehicle**, because the
quantity that would have settled it, turnaround, was never measured.

### What It Fed Into

**The engine outlived the vehicle by years as a technology project and then closed too.** The ablative
low-cost approach did not become the standard route to a cheap engine.

**What did become the standard route is visible in what replaced the whole programme's premise.** The
decision history that produced this whole family of programmes is set out in
[Heppenheimer's account of the shuttle decision][book_the_space_shuttle_decision]. The reduction in launch
cost that the reusable launch vehicle programme was chartered to pursue did arrive, and it arrived through
recovering and reflying an expensive engine many times rather than through building a cheap one to throw
away.
**The X-34's bet was that the way to make launch cheap is to make the hardware cheap. The bet that paid was that the way to make launch cheap is to use expensive hardware more often.**

**That is worth stating carefully rather than triumphally.** The two strategies are not opposites and a
small launcher today may well be right to use a simple engine. What can be said is that the specific
inference the X-34 rested on, that cheap hardware implies cheap access, was not the one that turned out to
matter most.

### What It Failed to Influence

**The two airframes are the most direct evidence of influence, and they went to a scrapyard.** They sat at
the flight research centre, moved to a desert airfield, then to a crane company's yard, and were at a
scrapyard before 2020.
**A vehicle that is ninety percent finished and then abandoned teaches nothing to anybody, because nothing was learned from it that was written down.**
The programme appears in [the agency's own history of the X-vehicles][ref_xvehicles] as a vehicle that was
built and did not fly.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

### Cost Is Not an Engineering Quantity and This Article Treats It as One

**The whole analysis above prices simplifications in seconds, kilograms and newtons, and then sets the result beside dollars.**
Those are not commensurable. A gas generator that costs 17.86 seconds of specific impulse is a fact. Whether
that trade was worth making depends on a price nobody published for a chamber nobody built in quantity.

**The honest position is that this article can compute what simplification cost in physics and cannot compute what it saved in money**,
and every conclusion about the trade is therefore one-sided.

### The Cost Comparison Has a Denominator Problem

**Dividing programme cost by vehicle mass is a crude instrument and the numbers move a great deal with the choice.**
Dividing by the number of airframes built gives a different answer. Dividing by flights achieved gives
infinity for both.
**The mass denominator was chosen because both programmes published a mass, and no denominator would have made the comparison rigorous.**

### The Review Might Simply Have Been Right

**This article has treated the 305 percent growth as the price of restoring what low-cost planning removed. There is a less flattering reading and it deserves stating.**
The original estimate may have been wrong on its own terms rather than deliberately thin, and a programme
that underestimates by a factor of four has a competence problem rather than a philosophy.

**The record does not distinguish these**, and the two readings differ in what they imply. Under the first,
low-cost demonstration is a coherent strategy that must budget for eventual rigour. Under the second, the
X-34 is simply a badly estimated project and there is no general lesson at all.

### The Comparison With the X-33 Flatters the X-34

**The two vehicles were not trying to do the same thing and the per-pound comparison quietly assumes they were.**
The X-33 was attempting a mass fraction nobody had achieved with technologies nobody had built. The X-34 was
attempting a flight profile within reach of existing practice.
**A programme attempting something harder should cost more, and some of the ratio is that rather than efficiency.**

## The Contemporary Literature

**The subjects this article computes are all active, and two of them are more active now than they were then, for reasons the programme would have found ironic.**

### Ablative Materials and Their Modelling

**The ablation modelling the article treats as a recession rate is now a detailed thermochemical subject**,
with pyrolysis, char and surface chemistry resolved rather than lumped, and it is driven largely by
planetary entry rather than by cheap engines.

### Low-Cost Propulsion, Which Came Back Through Manufacture

**The X-34's answer to expensive engines was to make a cheap one badly on purpose. The modern answer is to make an expensive one quickly**,
with additive manufacturing collapsing the part count and the lead time of exactly the regeneratively cooled
chamber the Fastrac avoided. **The constraint the Fastrac was designed around has largely dissolved**, which
is the second time in two articles that a 1990s architecture has been overtaken by a change in how things
are made rather than in how they work.

### Air Launch, Which Has Since Been Settled Commercially and Mostly Against Itself

**The draft of this article said the argument for air launch was still being had. That is too kind, because the market has spent the last decade running the experiment.**

**The operating method the X-34 borrowed was already commercial when the programme started**, and the
air-launched booster that supplied it flew for decades at a cost per kilogram that never came down to the
promise.
**A later attempt put a liquid-fuelled orbital rocket under a widebody airliner and flew it six times between 2020 and 2023.**
Five of the six reached orbit.
**The operator went bankrupt in April 2023 and ceased operations the following month**, its assets sold at
auction for something near thirty-six million dollars, and the carrier aircraft was bought by another
company and turned to hypersonic flight testing rather than to launch.

**Reaching orbit was not the problem. Five flights out of six did that.** What failed was the thing the X-34
existed to demonstrate.

**That is a harder verdict on the X-34's premise than anything in the programme's own record**, and it
should be stated with its limits. One company failing is a fact about one company.
**But the specific claim, that removing the launch pad removes enough cost to change the economics, has now been tested with real money by people who believed it**,
and the answer that came back was the same one the restructure plan gave in 2000.
**The infrastructure a vehicle does not build is not where the cost is.**

**The literature on small launch economics is where this argument now lives**, and it is a great deal larger
than the air-launch literature that preceded it.

### Autonomy, Landing and the Risk Case

**The unvalidated automatic landing that helped end the programme is now routine**, and it is routine
because vehicles fly it repeatedly rather than because anybody proved it on paper.
**That is the X-34's own risk argument resolved by the method the X-34 could not afford.**

**The vehicle's own cluster holds no contemporary records at all, and this is the second consecutive article for which that is true.**
Every record carrying the X-34 designation predates 2002, exactly as every record carrying the X-33's did.
**Two instances make it a pattern rather than an anecdote.** A cancelled programme stops generating
literature under its own name almost immediately, which means the documentary trace of a vehicle is not a
measure of what it contributed but of how long it survived.

## The Source Base

**This article rests on 2,227 references published through 2001, when the programme was cancelled, and 3,698 published from 2015 onward.**
Every harvested record is cited.

### Both Halves, Counted and Not Only Divided

**A reference pass that reports fractions alone will misdescribe itself, and this article was built in passes that would have misdescribed themselves in opposite directions.**

| | After drafting | After the primary pass | After the contemporary pass |
|---|---|---|---|
| Research references cited | 3,227 | 4,270 | 6,295 |
| Period through 2001 | 1,236, 38.3% | 2,227, 52.2% | 2,227, 35.4% |
| Contemporary 2015 onward | 1,664, 51.6% | 1,673, 39.2% | 3,698, 58.7% |
| Published 2022 onward | 793, 24.6% | 793, 18.6% | 1,897, 30.1% |
| Report literature | 661, 20.5% | 884, 20.7% | 884, 14.0% |

**Read the counts and the fractions together, because each pass moved one and not the other.** The primary
pass added 991 period records while the contemporary count rose by nine,
**and the contemporary fraction fell twelve points.** The contemporary pass then added 2,025 modern records
and **the period count did not move at all**, while the period fraction fell seventeen.

**Nothing was ever removed. In both directions it was the denominator that moved.** The report literature is
the clearest case,
**holding at exactly 884 records across the final pass while its share fell from 20.7 percent to 14.0**,
which is a fact about how much else was added and about nothing whatever to do with the reports.

### What the Equation Pass Did to the Reference Base

**Writing the relations down changed which literature the article needs, and an audit of the seventeen subjects the equations name found thirteen thin and six at zero.**
Among the zeroes were
**the convective heat transfer correlation the article displays and the effective heat of ablation it inverts for**,
which is the central quantity of the whole ablation section.

**None of those was thin because the literature is thin.** The earlier harvests asked for ablative
materials, low-cost engines and air launch,
**and before the equations existed the article had no reason to ask for gas-side heat transfer coefficients, transpiration cooling or mass injection into a boundary layer.**
Harvesting in the period's own vocabulary took the heat transfer heading from one record to twenty-eight and
the transpiration heading from nine to forty-two.

### Three Subjects That Stay Thin, and Why

**The rocket equation returns nothing at all in a pool of four thousand three hundred, and neither does the ascent loss budget.**
That is not a gap in the harvest. **It is a thin heading over a subject nobody writes papers about**,
because both live in every textbook and in no journal article. A search for them is a search for a
literature that does not exist in that form.

**The effective heat of ablation returns two records**, which is the same phenomenon in a milder form, since
the quantity is discussed throughout the ablation literature under the vocabulary of char layers, blowing
parameters and surface energy balances rather than under its own name.

**Reporting these rather than padding them is the point.** A subject can be thin because the work was never
done, because the heading is wrong, or because the knowledge is so settled that it stopped generating
papers. **These three are the third kind**, and the third kind is invisible to a count.

### What Counts as Primary Here

**The programme window is 1996 to 2001 and it is short.** Within it the primary record is the engine's
development literature, which is substantial because a government laboratory built the engine and published,
and the airframe literature, which is thinner because a company built the airframe and did not.

**That asymmetry is the same one the X-32 article found and it points the other way here.** The engine is
documented like a research project because it was one. The vehicle is documented like a contract deliverable
because it was one.
**Two halves of a single programme, and the half a research agency owned is the half that left a literature.**

### The Ablation Literature Is Older Than the Programme

**A second primary base sits well before 1996.** Ablative chamber and nozzle materials were characterised
from the late 1950s onward, largely for solid rocket motors, and a 1960s report on throat erosion is a
primary source for this article's recession estimate in a way that a 2020 planetary entry study is not.

### What the Record Does Not Contain

**The cost of a Fastrac combustion chamber in production is not in the public record**, and it is the single
number that would decide whether the ablative choice was economically right.
**The article computes everything around that hole and says where the hole is.**

### The Period Base in Full

**Every record harvested for this article is cited, and the ones the argument did not reach individually are listed here by subject rather than discarded.**
A source retrieved and never used is work done and thrown away. These are the period records, meaning
everything published before 2015, and the contemporary half is listed in the section above.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The X-34 contract was awarded to Orbital Sciences in 1996 at a figure near 86 million dollars. The Fastrac
engine, also designated MC-1, was developed by the agency's Marshall centre, used a gas generator cycle and
an ablatively cooled chamber and nozzle, and was fired for up to 155 seconds. The first airframe rolled out
in 1999 and made captive flights beneath the carrier aircraft in June and September of that year. A second
airframe was mated to the carrier in 2000. No free flight, powered or unpowered, was ever made. A joint
review in 2000 identified inadequate system testing, single-string avionics and unvalidated automatic
landing among the risks, and a restructure plan put the total requirement near 348 million dollars. The
programme was cancelled on 31 March 2001 alongside the X-33. The two airframes passed through storage and a
private yard and reached a scrapyard before 2020.

### Engineering Analysis

The specific impulse of 296.14 seconds implied by thrust over total flow, the recovered gas generator
fraction of 5.69 percent, and the 17.86 second impulse penalty are this article's arithmetic on three
published figures, and the identity that the fractional impulse penalty equals the fractional flow diversion
is exact and was tested over twenty thousand randomised inputs. The 148 second burn time and its 1.047
margin against the longest published test are arithmetic on published masses and flow. The throat area,
throat diameter and thrust coefficient depend on an assumed characteristic velocity of 1,780 metres per
second. The liner recession figures depend on an assumed recession rate and are presented as a range rather
than a value. The air-launch energy donation of 531.9 metres per second and the 16.0 percent thrust recovery
depend on assumed release conditions and an assumed area ratio. The bulk densities and the 2.982 ratio are
arithmetic on published densities.
**The result that the gauge-limited tank fraction goes as one over the radius is derived here, and the finding that the ratio between two propellant systems is exactly the inverse of their bulk density ratio is an identity rather than a coincidence.**

### Inference

**That the 305 percent growth measures the price of restoring what low-cost planning removed is an inference**,
and the competing reading, that the original estimate was simply wrong, is set out in the Where the Framing
Breaks Down section and is not excluded by anything in the record.

**That the X-34's ablative chamber was a defensible economic choice is not asserted**, because the number
that would decide it was never published.

**That a small demonstrator cannot stand in for a large vehicle's tank fraction is an inference from the minimum gauge argument**,
and it assumes the X-34's tanks were built to the same minimum gauge as the previous article's, which the
record does not state.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Whether the X-34 would have flown successfully is not settled.** Nothing had failed. Nothing had been
demonstrated either.

**Whether rapid turnaround was achievable is not settled and could only have been settled by flying.**

**The production cost of the engine's consumable chamber is not settled**, and it is the hinge of the entire
ablative trade.

**The tank radius used in the scaling comparison is assumed rather than published**, and the comparison
moves with it, though the direction of the conclusion does not.

## Out of Scope

The detailed thermochemistry of ablation. The carrier aircraft and its modification. The Pegasus booster
from which the operating method descends. The X-33, treated in the previous article. The Space Launch
Initiative that absorbed both programmes. The disposal history of the airframes beyond the fact of it. The
commercial position of the contractor.

## Conclusion

**The X-34 was cancelled because somebody finally priced the risk.**

Nothing broke. No structure failed a test, no engine failed a firing, no aerodynamic surprise appeared.
**What happened is that a programme built to be cheap was asked what it would cost to fly safely, and the answer was four times what it had been given.**

**The things that made it cheap and the things that made it unflyable were the same things.** Single-string
avionics, thin system testing and an unvalidated automatic landing are exactly what a low-cost demonstrator
deletes, and exactly what must be restored before anyone drops a rocket aeroplane over inhabited ground.
**The cost was never removed. It was deferred, and the deferral carried interest of 305 percent.**

**Set beside the previous article the pair is exact and inverted.** The X-33's binding quantity was mass,
which obeys a conservation law, and its demonstrator returned a reading that did not close. The X-34's
binding quantity was cost, which obeys nothing, and its demonstrator returned a revised estimate.
**One programme was killed by a number it measured. The other was killed by a number it recalculated.**

**The physics the cost argument left behind does compute, and it mostly says the choices were sound.** The
gas generator costs 5.69 percent of the propellant and exactly 5.69 percent of the impulse. The kerosene the
vehicle burned is 2.982 times denser than the hydrogen the X-33 carried, which rescues a small vehicle from
the minimum-gauge penalty that its size imposes. Air launch donates under six percent of an orbital energy
budget and recovers 16.0 percent of the engine's thrust, so the benefit usually claimed for it is the
smaller one.
**And the ablative chamber, the emblem of the whole approach, made a reusable vehicle that consumed a combustion chamber every flight.**

**This series has now met a designation marking an absence of demand in the [X-27][related_post_a324_lockheed_x27], an absence of knowledge in the [X-30][related_post_a327_rockwell_x30], an answer nobody wanted in the [X-33][related_post_a330_lockheed_martin_x33], and here a vehicle that was finished, was never asked a question it could fail, and was scrapped.**
Of the four it is the only one that was ready.
